implementation_notes: .NET gives a real instrument: `dotnet list package --include-transitive` for the dependency half, and the compiler's CS0169/CS0414/CS8321 warnings plus an IDE 'unnecessary usages' inspection for fields and private members. The C#-specific anchor is reflection-based registration and `IHttpClientFactory`/DI registrations that keep a type reachable without a compile-time reference — which is exactly why an 'unused' class injected into a container is not necessarily dead. Partial classes are the other: splitting a type across files can hide an anchor in a file nobody opens.
idiom_name: unused NuGet package, unused partial, unused event handler
pitfalls: A package listed but never imported is invisible to code review and carries its own CVE surface.
Types resolved only by DI or by reflection are live and unreferenced; the compiler cannot tell you.
`[Obsolete]` on an anchor keeps the type compiling, so the warning is a plan rather than a removal — pair it with a version and a removal date.
